answer.rationale: The incumbent has refused to reopen price and the mandate for an 18% cut is non-negotiable this cycle, so renewing or further negotiating is unlikely to meet the objective. The primary contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew, so deferring risks an unplanned supply gap while the line is already at 94% committed volume with zero buffer—unacceptable given the no-increase-in-delivery-risk constraint. Memory_c2 indicates a prior switch to a low-cost vendor delivered quick onboarding and accurate invoicing, supporting feasibility, while memory_c3 shows second-sourcing effectively mitigated single-point-of-failure risk during a shortage, suggesting a phased or guarded transition can control risk. Given the tight capacity buffer, I intend to move toward the low-cost vendor as primary but structure the initial cutover as a small guarded test (e.g., partial volume or short initial term) rather than a full immediate switch, to validate delivery reliability before committing the whole volume. This flags real downstream risk (transition disruption, unproven long-term quality/lead-time under full load) and preserves uncertainty about whether the low-cost vendor can sustain reliability at full committed volume before scaling further next cycle.
